Sure
shŭr
adj. (firm, stable, not liable to fail; in Scripture said of God's foundation, God's testimony, and the believer's hope)
From Old French sur, from Latin securus — se- (without) plus cura (care), that is, free from anxiety. English kept the outward sense of firmness; the Latin root remembers the inward sense of a mind at rest, and Scripture joins the two.

Biblical Definition

Sure in the Authorized Version is a load-bearing word: it describes what will hold when weight is put on it. It is said of the foundation: “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation” (Isa 28:16), the prophecy Peter and Paul both apply to Christ; and again, “the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his” (2Ti 2:19) — a verse that grounds the perseverance of the saints in God's knowledge rather than in the believer's grip. It is said of the Scriptures: “the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple” (Psa 19:7) — sure enough that a simple man may build on it without a scholar's help. And it is said of hope: “which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil” (Heb 6:19) — an anchor thrown not downward into the seabed but upward into the holy of holies, where Christ has already gone.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines sure as certain, unfailing, infallible — and also as firm, stable, secure, not liable to failure, loss or change.

expand to see more

SURE, a. Certain; unfailing; infallible.

We have also a more sure word of prophecy. 2 Pet. i.

2. Certainly knowing, or having full confidence. I am sure that ye are not of us.

3. Firm; stable; steady; not liable to failure, loss or change.

4. Safe; being in no danger. Fear not, thou art sure.

Key Scripture

2Ti 2:19 — "Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity."

Isa 28:16 — "Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste."

Psa 19:7 — "The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple."

Heb 6:19 — "Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;"

Modern Corruption

2Ti 2:19 is quoted for comfort while its second half is dropped, producing an assurance detached from the departing-from-iniquity that Paul makes its companion seal.

expand to see more

Paul stamps the foundation with two inscriptions, not one. The first is God's side: The Lord knoweth them that are his — election, and therefore a security no failure of the believer's memory or nerve can undo. The second is the believer's side: Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity. Quote the first alone and you get the bare once-saved-always-saved slogan the dictionary rejects; quote the second alone and you get a religion of self-watching. The Reformed doctrine is perseverance, which holds both: God preserves His own, and the mark that He is doing so is that they depart from iniquity.

Psa 19:7 answers the parallel corruption about Scripture. The testimony of the LORD is sure, and its effect is to make the simple wise — not the trained, not the credentialed, the simple. The doctrine of perspicuity stands on verses like this one: the plain man with a plain Bible may know what he must know for salvation and obedience. That is why the Reformers put the text in the common tongue, and why any scheme requiring the layman to wait on the expert before he may be sure of anything is a step back toward the darkness they left.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin securus, free from care; rendering Hebrew aman (H539), to be firm or faithful — the root of amen — and Greek bebaios (G949), firm, and stereos (G4731), solid.

expand to see more

Latin securus — se- without + cura care; the same root gives English secure.

Hebrew aman (H539) — to support, be firm, be faithful; the root behind amen, and behind “the testimony of the LORD is sure” (Psa 19:7).

Hebrew musad musad — “a sure foundation” in Isa 28:16 is a doubled participle: founded, founded — a foundation that has been laid and laid firmly.

Greek bebaios (G949) — firm, steadfast; the anchor “sure and stedfast” of Heb 6:19.

Greek stereos (G4731) — solid, hard; “the foundation of God standeth sure” (2Ti 2:19), the word behind English stereo in its old sense of solidity.

Usage

"“The foundation of God standeth sure” — sealed on both sides, God's knowing and the believer's departing."

"“A sure foundation” — a stone laid and laid firmly, applied by the apostles to Christ."

"“An anchor of the soul… sure and stedfast” — thrown upward, within the veil."
